sections.title: All Evidence is Not Equal
sections.content: In debate, the quality of your evidence matters as much as the argument itself. Judges are trained to evaluate source credibility. The source hierarchy ranks evidence types by reliability.
bullets: Level 1 — Peer-reviewed academic studies and government reports
Level 2 — Major news organizations with editorial standards
Level 3 — Expert opinions and think tank reports
Level 5 — Social media and anonymous sources

sections.title: When to Use Each Level
sections.content: Higher-level sources are always preferable, but sometimes you need lower-level sources for timeliness or specific data. Learn to cite the highest level available and be transparent about limitations.
bullets: Academic studies carry the most weight with judges
Government data is considered highly reliable
News articles are good for recent events
Blogs should only support, never prove, a claim

sections.title: Evaluating Sources
sections.content: Compare three citations on the same topic:
sections.good: A 2024 meta-analysis in Nature (peer-reviewed) found a 15% reduction in carbon emissions from the policy. — High quality.
sections.bad: A Reddit post claims the policy reduced emissions. — Low quality, anonymous.
sections.explanation: In a debate, the first citation would outweigh the second. Always ask: Who published this? What is their methodology? When was it published?

sections.instruction: Rank these sources from highest to lowest credibility.
steps: Peer-reviewed study in a scientific journal
Government report from an official agency
sections.feedback: Academic > Government > News > Opinion > Social Media

sections.q: Why do peer-reviewed studies rank highest in the source hierarchy?
options: They undergo expert review and methodological scrutiny before publication
They are longer than other sources
sections.explain: Peer review means independent experts have evaluated the methodology and conclusions before publication.

sections.statement: A recent news article should always be preferred over an academic study from 5 years ago.
sections.feedback: Timeliness matters but does not override quality. A peer-reviewed study from 5 years ago is often more reliable than a breaking news report.

sections.sentence: In the source hierarchy, {0}-reviewed studies and government reports are the most credible.
sections.feedback: Peer-reviewed studies undergo expert scrutiny before publication.

questions.q: What question should you ask first when evaluating a source?
options: Who published this and what are their credentials?
questions.feedback: Source credibility begins with the publisher's expertise and methodology.
